passages.happening: ‘Now these were the ones who sealed the document: Nehemiah the governor, son of Hacaliah, and also Zedekiah’ (verse 1). Then come the priests (verses 2-8), the Levites (verses 9-13), and the leaders of the people (verses 14-27), name after name.
passages.hearers:
Chapters 8 to 10 move from hearing God's word, to confessing sin, to commitment. This chapter is the commitment, and it begins with the names of those who put their seals to it.

A document in the ancient Near East was made binding by sealing it, often by pressing a personal seal into clay or wax attached to it. A seal was a person's signature. By sealing the agreement, the leaders made the pledge a public and legal act for which they could be held to account.

Many of the names appear elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah. Several of the priestly names match priestly families listed in chapter 12, and several of the leaders' names match family names from the register of returnees in chapter 7, such as Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam and Zattu. That suggests that some seals were placed by heads of families on behalf of whole clans.

Nehemiah's name comes first. The governor binds himself before he binds anyone else.
passages.later: The same family names stand in the first list of returnees: ‘the descendants of Parosh, 2,172’ (Ezra 2:3).
passages.asks: The leaders signed first. Ask what you are willing to put your own name to before you ask it of others. And ask whose names stand behind the faith you have received.

passages.t: The pledge: marriage, the Sabbath, and the house of God
passages.happening:
The rest of the people, priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, ‘and all who had separated themselves from the people of the land to obey the Law of God’ (verse 28), with their wives and their children old enough to understand, join their leaders. They ‘commit themselves with a sworn oath to follow the Law of God given through His servant Moses’ (verse 29).

Then the promises are spelled out. ‘We will not give our daughters in marriage to the people of the land, and we will not take their daughters for our sons’ (verse 30). They will not buy grain or goods from traders on the Sabbath or holy days, and ‘Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow, and will cancel every debt’ (verse 31).

They pledge a third of a shekel a year for the service of the house of God (verse 32), for the bread, the offerings and the feasts (verse 33). They cast lots for families to bring wood for the altar at set times (verse 34). They will bring their firstfruits, their firstborn, and a tenth of their produce for the Levites (verses 35-38). The pledge ends, ‘Thus we will not neglect the house of our God’ (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
Notice who joins: not only those born to Israel, but ‘all who had separated themselves from the people of the land to obey the Law of God’ (verse 28). As at the Passover in Ezra 6, the community includes outsiders who had turned to the LORD.

Swearing with an oath meant calling a curse on oneself if one broke the promise, a serious act in a culture that took such words as binding.

Each promise applies a part of the law of Moses. The marriage pledge echoes Deuteronomy 7, which forbade marriage with the peoples of Canaan because it would lead Israel to serve other gods. The Sabbath pledge meets a new situation: the law forbade work on the Sabbath, and the people now apply it to buying goods brought in by traders who did not keep it. The seventh year, when fields lay fallow and debts were cancelled, was a costly promise for a poor farming people.

The offerings describe the temple's regular worship: the twelve loaves set out each Sabbath, the daily and festival sacrifices, and the tithes that supported the Levites, who had no land of their own. The house of God is named again and again, and it closes the chapter. That is where the weight of the document falls.

These promises matter for what comes later. When Nehemiah returns in chapter 13, he finds the people breaking almost exactly these pledges: about the temple's support, the Sabbath and marriage.
passages.later:
Behind the yearly gift stands the law of Exodus: ‘Everyone who crosses over to those counted must pay a half shekel’ (Exodus 30:13). In the Gospels, the collectors of the two-drachma tax for the temple ask Peter, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” (Matthew 17:24).

And the tithe for the Levites is the law of Numbers: ‘Behold, I have given to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance in return for the work they do’ (Numbers 18:21).
passages.hard:
Why do some of the pledges differ from what the law of Moses says?

Several promises go beyond or differ from the written law. Exodus 30 required a half shekel from each man counted in a census, but the people here pledge a third of a shekel every year. The law says the altar fire must never go out, but it does not set up a system for supplying wood by lot. And the law did not say in so many words that Israelites could not buy from foreigners on the Sabbath.

Interpreters explain these differences in a few ways. The third of a shekel may reflect a different shekel standard in the Persian period, a reduction for a poor community, or a new yearly gift distinct from the census tax. The wood offering and the Sabbath rule are generally seen as careful applications of the law to practical needs, so that its commands could actually be kept.

This kind of application was not seen as adding to God's word but as working out how to obey it. The chapter shows a community trying in good faith to put its promises into concrete form.
passages.asks: The people did not only promise to obey; they wrote down what obeying would cost them. Ask what your faith would look like if you put it into specific promises. And ask what you might be neglecting in the house of God, the shared life and worship of your church.
